[[File:Afghanistan Population 1950-2021 Forecast 2022-2032 UN World Population Prospects 2022.svg|thumb|350px|Population, [[fertility rate]] and [[net reproduction rate]], United Nations estimates]]

As of 2025, [[Afghanistan]] has an estimated [[Population (human biology)|population]] of around 49.5 million people.<ref name="population clock: world">{{Cite web |title=Population Clock:World – Afghanistan |url=https://www.census.gov/popclock/world/af#world-footer}}</ref> The country is characterized by a highly diverse, [[Multinational state|multi-ethnic]], and [[Multilingualism|multilingual]] society, reflecting its historical position at the crossroads of [[Central Asia|Central]], [[South Asia|South]], and [[West Asia|Western Asia]], along ancient trade and invasion routes. The four major ethnic categories in the country are [[Pashtuns|Pashtun]], [[Tajiks|Tajik]]/[[Farsiwan]], [[Hazaras|Hazara]], and [[Uzbeks|Uzbek]]. In addition, Afghanistan has a plethora of minor ethnic categories, including [[Pashayi people|Pashayi]],  [[Nuristanis|Nuristani]], [[Sikhism in Afghanistan|Sikh]], [[Hindkowans|Hindkowan]], [[Turkmens|Turkmen]], [[Kyrgyz in Afghanistan|Kyrgyz]], [[Baloch people in Afghanistan|Baloch]], [[Aimaq people|Aimaq]], [[Qizilbash]], [[History of Arabs in Afghanistan|Arab]] and many others.<ref>{{cite journal |id={{ProQuest|1304280677}} |last1=Iwamura |first1=Shinobu |title=Hunting for the Génghis Khanid Mongols in Afghanistan |journal=Japan Quarterly |volume=3 |issue=2 |date=April 1956 |pages=213 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://celcar.indiana.edu/materials/language-portal/mongolian/index.html | title=Mongolian | access-date=10 May 2024 | archive-date=10 December 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231210211448/https://celcar.indiana.edu/materials/language-portal/mongolian/index.html | url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://celt.indiana.edu/portal/Mongolian/index.html | title=Mongolian }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.britannica.com/summary/Mongolian-languages | title=Mongolian languages summary &#124; Britannica }}</ref><ref name="Critics: New Categories on Afghan IDs Will Incite Ethnic Tension">{{cite news |url=https://tolonews.com/afghanistan-170741 |title=Critics: New Categories on Afghan IDs Will Incite Ethnic Tension |publisher=TOLOnews |date=17 March 2021 |access-date=17 March 2021}}</ref><ref name="Factbook"/><ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2016/04/21/what-chance-for-afghanistan/|title=What Chance for Afghanistan?|first=Anatol|last=Lieven|date=21 April 2016|magazine=The New York Review of Books|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160422124057/https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2016/04/21/what-chance-for-afghanistan/|archive-date=22 April 2016}}</ref>

Approximately 43% of the population was under the age of 15, and about 74% of Afghans lived in rural areas as of 2016.<ref name="uis.unesco.org">{{cite web|url=https://uis.unesco.org/country/af|title=Afghanistan|date=27 November 2016 |publisher=UNESCO|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170510121322/http://uis.unesco.org/country/AF|archive-date=10 May 2017}}</ref> The country has one of the highest [[total fertility rate|fertility rates]] in the world outside of [[Africa]], with the average woman giving birth to five children over her lifetime. Around 6.8% of infants die during childbirth or early infancy.<ref name="uis.unesco.org"/> According to the [[World Health Organization]] (WHO), the nation's average [[life expectancy]] was estimated at about 63 years as of 2019.<ref name="WHO">{{cite web |title=Afghanistan |url=https://apps.who.int/gho/data/node.main.688 |access-date=1 March 2021 |publisher=World Health Organization (WHO)}}</ref><ref name="UNPD">{{cite web |year=2020 |title=Afghanistan |url=http://hdr.undp.org/en/countries/profiles/AFG |access-date=1 March 2021 |publisher=United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)}}</ref> The prevalence of [[HIV]] remains very low, affecting only about 0.04% of the population.<ref name="Factbook"/>

[[Pashto]] ({{lang|ps|پښتو}}) and [[Dari]] ({{lang|prs|دری}}) are the [[official languages]] of Afghanistan.<ref name="Constitution" /> Dari serves as the inter-ethnic [[lingua franca]] across most of the country, particularly in northern and eastern provinces as well as in most major cities. Pashto is predominantly spoken in regions south of the [[Hindu Kush]] mountains and extends eastward toward the [[Indus River]] in neighbouring [[Pakistan]]. Smaller languages such as [[Uzbek language|Uzbek]] and [[Turkmen language|Turkmen]] are spoken in parts of northern Afghanistan.<ref name="Factbook" /> Multilingualism is widespread, particularly in the major urban centres.

Up to 89.7% of the population adheres to [[Sunni Islam]] and follows the [[Hanafi]] school of [[Fiqh|Islamic jurisprudence]], while between 10% and 15% are followers of [[Shia Islam in Afghanistan|Shia Islam]], with the majority belonging to the [[Twelver]] branch, and smaller communities adhering to [[Ismailism|Ismaili]] traditions.<ref name="Factbook"/><ref name="Pew"/> The remaining 0.3% of the population practices other religions, including Sikhism and [[Hinduism in Afghanistan|Hinduism]]. Outside the principal urban centres, much of the population is organized into tribal or other kinship-based groups that maintain their own traditional customs.

== Population size and distribution ==
{{Further|Afghan diaspora}}
Anatol Lieven of [[Georgetown University in Qatar]] wrote in 2021 that "it may be noted that in the whole of modern Afghan history there has never been a census that could be regarded as remotely reliable."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Lieven|first=Anatol|title=An Afghan Tragedy: The Pashtuns, the Taliban and the State|journal=[[Survival (journal)|Survival: Global Politics and Strategy]]|volume=63|year=2021|issue=3 |pages=7–36|doi=10.1080/00396338.2021.1930403|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Historical ===
[[File:Afghans at Ghazi Stadium in 2011.jpg|thumb|[[Sport in Afghanistan|Sport]] fans inside the [[Ghazi Stadium]] in the capital of [[Kabul]], which is [[multiethnic society|multi-ethnic]] and the largest city of Afghanistan.]]
The first and only nationwide census of Afghanistan was carried out in 1979. It revealed a population of 13,051,358 (rural 11,037,231, urban 2,014,127).<ref>{{Cite web |title=DEMOGRAPHIC YEARBOOK 1983 |url=https://unstats.un.org/unsd/demographic-social/products/dyb/dybsets/1983%20DYB.pdf |website=unstats.un.org}}</ref> Previously there had been scattered attempts to conduct censuses in individual cities.<ref>[http://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/census-ii CENSUS ii. In Afghanistan] [[Encyclopædia Iranica]]</ref> According to the 1876 census, [[Kabul]] had a population of 140,700 people.<ref>(Gazetteer of Afghanistan VI, p. 333).</ref> In [[Kandahar]] in 1891 a population census was carried out, according to which 31,514 people lived in the city, of which 16,064 were men and 15,450 were women.<ref>Kandahar Newsletter, 10 August 1891, IOR L/P & S/7/63/1295</ref>

From 1979 until the end of 1983, some 5 million people left the country to take shelter in neighbouring northwestern Pakistan and eastern Iran. This exodus was largely unchecked by any government. The Afghan government in 1983 reported a population of 15.96&nbsp;million, which presumably included the exodus.<ref name="U.S. Library of Congress">{{cite web |url=https://countrystudies.us/afghanistan/36.htm |title=Population |publisher=U.S. Library of Congress |year=2008 |access-date=12 October 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.wikiwix.com/cache/20110719220830/https://countrystudies.us/afghanistan/36.htm |archive-date=19 July 2011 }}</ref>

It is assumed that roughly 600,000 to as high as 2 million Afghans may have been killed during the various 1979–2001 wars.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://necrometrics.com/20c1m.htm#Afghanistan |title=Afghanistan (1979–2001) |access-date=12 October 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110305175626/https://necrometrics.com/20c1m.htm#Afghanistan |archive-date=5 March 2011 }}</ref> These figures are questionable and no attempt has ever been made to verify if they were actually killed or had moved to neighbouring countries as refugees.<ref name="U.S. Library of Congress"/>

As no census has been performed after 1979 and millions of people may have left the country, the current population of Afghanistan can only be guessed.

=== Current and latest ===
As of 2021, the total population of Afghanistan is around 37.5 million,<ref name="Factbook">{{cite web |url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/afghanistan/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210104184342/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/afghanistan/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=4 January 2021 |title=Afghanistan |work=The World Factbook |publisher=CIA |access-date=1 March 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.worldometers.info/world-population/afghanistan-population/ |title=Afghanistan |work=Worldmeters |publisher=worldmeters.info |access-date=30 May 2019}}</ref> which includes the 3 million Afghan nationals living in both [[Afghans in Pakistan|Pakistan]] and [[Afghans in Iran|Iran]].<ref name="PAN-pop"/> About 26% of the population is [[urban area|urbanite]] and the remaining 74% lives in rural areas.<ref name="Factbook"/>

Afghanistan's [[Central Statistics Organization]] (CSO) stated in 2011 that the total number of Afghans living inside Afghanistan was about 26 million<ref name="PAN-pop">{{cite news |url=https://www.pajhwok.com/en/2011/11/20/afghanistans-population-reaches-26m |title=Afghanistan's population reaches 26m |publisher=Pajhwok Afghan News |editor=Mohammad Jawad Sharifzada |date=20 November 2011 |access-date=5 December 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130101074433/https://www.pajhwok.com/en/2011/11/20/afghanistans-population-reaches-26m |archive-date=1 January 2013}}</ref> and by 2017 it reached 29.2&nbsp;million. Of this, 15 million are males and 14.2&nbsp;million are females.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://pajhwok.com/photo/afghan-population-29-2-million/ |title=Afghan Population 29.2 Million |website=pajhwok.com|date=10 May 2017 |url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171011103545/https://www.pajhwok.com/en/node/483787|archive-date=11 October 2017|last1=Hamdard |first1=Azizullah }}</ref> The country's population is expected to reach 82 million by 2050.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.prb.org/Countries/Afghanistan.aspx |title=Afghanistan – Population Reference Bureau |publisher=[[Population Reference Bureau]] |access-date=29 December 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131202224051/http://www.prb.org/Countries/Afghanistan.aspx |archive-date=2 December 2013 }}</ref>

Urban areas have experienced rapid population growth in the last decade, which is due to the return of over 5 million [[expatriate|expats]]. The only city in Afghanistan with over a million residents is its capital, [[Kabul]].

=== Infant-related statistics ===
Afghanistan 2024 [[total fertility rate]] has been estimated at 4.4.
<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/field/total-fertility-rate/country-comparison/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251229225430/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/field/total-fertility-rate/country-comparison/|url-status=dead|archive-date=29 December 2025|title=Total fertility rate Comparison – The World Factbook|website=www.cia.gov}}</ref> In 2022 it was 4.5, about twice the world average rate.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.DYN.TFRT.IN?end=2022&start=1960&view=chart|title=World Bank Open Data|website=World Bank Open Data}}</ref> The rate has fallen since the early 1990s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.DYN.TFRT.IN?end=2022&locations=AF&start=1983&view=chart|title=World Bank Open Data|website=World Bank Open Data}}</ref>

The recent estimate in the above chart is somewhat supported by the below national [[opinion poll]]s, which were aimed at knowing how a group of about 804 to 8,706 local residents in Afghanistan felt about the current war, political situation, as well as the economic and social issues affecting their daily lives. == Languages ==
{{main article|Languages of Afghanistan}}

[[File:Map of Pashto-speaking areas in Afghanistan and Pakistan.svg|thumb|Map of Pashto-speaking areas in Afghanistan and Pakistan]]
[[Dari]] and [[Pashto]] are both [[official language]]s of Afghanistan.<ref name="Constitution">{{cite web|title=Article Sixteen of the Constitution of Afghanistan|url=https://www.afghan-web.com/politics/current_constitution.html#preamble|quote=From among the languages of Pashto, Dari, Uzbeki, Turkmani, Baluchi, Pashai, Nuristani, Pamiri (alsana), Arab and other languages spoken in the country, Pashto and Dari are the official languages of the state.|year=2004|access-date=25 July 2012|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131028065437/http://www.afghan-web.com/politics/current_constitution.html#preamble|archive-date=28 October 2013}}</ref>
[[Uzbek language|Uzbek]] and [[Turkmen language|Turkmen]] are spoken as native languages in northern provinces, mainly among the [[Uzbeks]] and [[Afghan Turkmens|Turkmens]]. Smaller number of Afghans are also fluent in [[English language|English]], [[Urdu]], [[Balochi language|Balochi]], [[Arabic language|Arabic]] and other languages. An approximate distribution of languages spoken in the country is shown in the chart below:

{{Clear}}
Based on information from the latest national opinion polls, up to 51% stated that they can speak or understand Pashto and up to 79% stated that they can speak or understand Dari. Uzbek was spoken or understood by up to 11% and Turkmen by up to 7%. Other languages that can be spoken are Arabic (4%) and Balochi (2%).<ref name="AsiaFoundation"/><ref name="ABCBBCARD"/>

== Religion ==
{{Main|Religion in Afghanistan}}

{{bar box
| titlebar=#ddd
| float=right
| title=[[Religion in Afghanistan]] (2015)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.thearda.com/internationalData/countries/Country_1_2.asp|title=Afghanistan, Religion and Social Profile|access-date=26 July 2021|archive-date=12 June 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210612032900/https://www.thearda.com/internationalData/countries/Country_1_2.asp|url-status=dead}}</ref>
| left1=Religion
| right1=Percent
| bars=
{{bar percent|[[Sunni Islam]]|Darkgreen|89.7}}
{{bar percent|[[Shia Islam]]|Green|10}}
{{bar percent|[[Religion in Afghanistan#Minority religious groups|others]]|blue|0.3}}
| caption=
}}

Almost the entire Afghan population is Muslim, with less than 1% being non-Muslim. Despite attempts to secularise Afghan society, Islamic practices pervade all aspects of life. Likewise, Islamic religious tradition and codes, together with traditional practices, provide the principal means of controlling personal conduct and settling legal disputes. Islam was used as the main basis for expressing opposition to the progressive reforms of Afghanistan by [[Amanullah Khan|King Amanullah]] in the 1920s.

The members of Sikh and Hindu communities are mostly concentrated in urban areas. They numbered hundreds of thousands in the 1970s but over 90% have since fled due to the Afghan wars and persecution.<ref>{{cite web|title=Nearly 99% Of Hindus, Sikhs Left Afghanistan in Last Three decades |publisher=TOLOnews|date=20 June 2016|url=https://tolonews.com/afghanistan/nearly-99-hindus-sikhs-left-afghanistan-last-three-decades}}</ref>
* '''[[Islam in Afghanistan|Islam]]''': 99.7% of the total population
** [[Sunni Muslim]]: 84.7–89.7%<ref name="Factbook" /><ref name="Pew">{{cite web|url=https://www.pewforum.org/2012/08/09/the-worlds-muslims-unity-and-diversity-1-religious-affiliation/#identity|title=Chapter 1: Religious Affiliation|date=9 August 2012|work=The World's Muslims: Unity and Diversity|publisher=[[Pew Research Center]]'s Religion & Public Life Project|access-date=4 September 2013|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161226113158/http://www.pewforum.org/2012/08/09/the-worlds-muslims-unity-and-diversity-1-religious-affiliation/#identity|archive-date=26 December 2016}}</ref>
** [[Shia Islam in Afghanistan|Shia Muslim]]: 7<ref name="Pew"/>-15%<ref name="Factbook" /><ref name="Pew" />
* '''[[Religion in Afghanistan#Minority religious groups|others]]''': 0.3%
** [[Baha'i Faith in Afghanistan|Baha'is]] In the hundreds
** [[Sikhism in Afghanistan|Sikhism]]: In the hundreds
** [[Hinduism in Afghanistan|Hinduism]]: In the hundreds
** [[Zoroastrianism]]: Unknown/unreported
** [[Christianity in Afghanistan|Christianity]]: Unknown
** [[History of the Jews in Afghanistan|Judaism]]: 0<ref>{{cite news |url=https://english.alaraby.co.uk/news/last-jew-afghanistan-en-route-us-report |title=Last Jew in Afghanistan en route to US: report |work=The New Arab |date=7 September 2021 |access-date=17 September 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/kabul-with-jewish-population-of-1-still-suffers-from-widespread-anti-semitism/|first=Ezzatullah|last=Mehrdad|access-date=9 September 2021|date=16 July 2019|work=The Times of Israel|title=Kabul, with Jewish population of 1, still suffers from widespread anti-Semitism}}</ref>
** [[Buddhism in Afghanistan|Buddhism]]: Unknown
